news_summary: Scientists have successfully expanded the genetic alphabet from 4 to 8 DNA letters, marking a breakthrough in synthetic biology.
news_summary_fr: Des scientifiques ont réussi à élargir l'alphabet génétique, passant de 4 à 8 lettres d'ADN, ce qui marque une avancée majeure dans le domaine de la biologie synthétique.
news_summary_es: Los científicos han logrado ampliar el alfabeto genético de 4 a 8 letras de ADN, lo que supone un gran avance en el campo de la biología sintética.

articles.title: Life uses 4 DNA letters. Scientists just made 8 work
articles.summary: Researchers at UC San Diego have demonstrated that a key cellular enzyme can accurately read an eight-letter genetic alphabet, doubling the four letters used by all known life on Earth. Detailed imaging revealed that RNA polymerase handles synthetic DNA letters in surprisingly similar ways to natural ones. The finding brings scientists closer to building expanded genetic systems that could perform entirely new biological functions.
articles.content:
All known life on Earth relies on the same four-letter genetic alphabet. Researchers at the University of California San Diego have now shown that one of biology's most important enzymes can accurately read and transcribe a much larger version containing eight genetic letters.

The finding suggests that cells can use their existing molecular machinery to handle synthetic genetic information. That marks an important step toward a long-standing goal in synthetic biology: expanding the language of DNA beyond the four letters found in nature. In the future, such systems could help scientists engineer biological machinery that carries out new functions or produces compounds that do not naturally exist.

How Cells Read an Eight-Letter Genetic Alphabet

The researchers focused on RNA polymerase, the enzyme that reads DNA and produces RNA -- the first step in gene expression. To see how the enzyme handles synthetic genetic information, the team combined biochemical experiments with high-resolution cryo-electron microscopy capable of revealing structures at scales smaller than the width of a single atom.

The researchers captured detailed structural views of RNA polymerase from Escherichia coli (E. coli) bacteria as it recognized and incorporated two synthetic base pairs. These artificial genetic letters are not found in nature.

The images showed that RNA polymerase identifies the synthetic DNA letters using many of the same biochemical and structural signals it relies on to recognize natural base pairs. That finding helps explain why the enzyme can accurately copy information written using an expanded genetic alphabet.

In a related study published in PNAS, the same research team found that RNA polymerase can also recognize another pair of synthetic base pairs even though they lack the hydrogen bonds that normally help hold DNA base pairs together.

Synthetic DNA Could Enable New Technologies

The potential applications extend well beyond understanding how DNA works. Earlier research has already used expanded genetic alphabets to create synthetic DNA molecules capable of recognizing liver cancer cells.

By showing in molecular detail how RNA polymerase reads and transcribes non-natural DNA letters, the new research provides an important foundation for technologies built around expanded genetic codes. Possible applications include new diagnostic tools, therapeutics, and engineered biological systems with capabilities that do not occur naturally.

Two Studies Explore Expanded Genetic Codes

The Nature Communications study ("Structural Basis of Transcription of the Hachimoji Eight-Letter Alphabet by E. coli RNA Polymerase"), led by Dong Wang, PhD, professor at the UC San Diego Skaggs School of Pharmacy and Pharmaceutical Sciences, was published on Sept. 2, 2026 in Nature Communications.

The PNAS study ("Hydrophobic unnatural base pair promotes trigger loop closure and catalysis in cellular RNA polymerase independent of hydrogen bonding"), published on Aug. 12, 2026, was also led by Wang.

This advancement has broad implications for synthetic biology, enabling the creation of new biological functions, diagnostics, and therapeutics, thus representing a meaningful positive impact on science and society.
articles.personality_title: Scientists expand DNA alphabet from 4 to 8 letters, showing key enzyme can read synthetic genes
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – All living things on Earth use DNA made of four letters: A, T, C, and G. These letters form the genetic code that tells cells how to work. Scientists have long wondered if it’s possible to add new letters to this code to create new kinds of life or tools.

**What happened** – Researchers at the University of California San Diego showed that an important enzyme called RNA polymerase can read DNA with eight letters instead of just four. They used special microscopes to look closely at how the enzyme reads two new synthetic base pairs that don’t exist in nature. The enzyme recognized these new letters almost the same way it does the natural ones.

**Impact** – This discovery means cells might use their normal machinery to work with new genetic codes. It opens the door to designing DNA with extra letters that could help scientists create medicines, detect diseases like cancer, or build new biological machines that do things natural life cannot.

**What's next step** – Scientists will continue to explore how these extra DNA letters can be used in living cells and develop new technologies based on expanded genetic codes. This could lead to breakthroughs in health, research, and synthetic biology.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Scientists have shown that a vital enzyme can read an eight-letter DNA alphabet, paving the way for new biological tools and medicines.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les scientifiques étendent l’alphabet de l’ADN de 4 à 8 lettres en montrant qu’une enzyme clé peut lire des gènes synthétiques
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Tous les êtres vivants sur Terre utilisent un ADN composé de quatre lettres : A, T, C et G. Ces lettres forment le code génétique qui indique aux cellules comment fonctionner. Les scientifiques se demandent depuis longtemps s’il est possible d’ajouter de nouvelles lettres à ce code pour créer de nouvelles formes de vie ou outils.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des chercheurs de l’Université de Californie à San Diego ont montré qu’une enzyme importante appelée ARN polymérase peut lire un ADN avec huit lettres au lieu de seulement quatre. Ils ont utilisé des microscopes spéciaux pour observer comment l’enzyme lit deux nouvelles paires de bases synthétiques qui n’existent pas dans la nature. L’enzyme a reconnu ces nouvelles lettres presque de la même manière que les naturelles.

**Impact** – Cette découverte signifie que les cellules pourraient utiliser leur machinerie normale pour travailler avec de nouveaux codes génétiques. Cela ouvre la voie à la conception d’ADN avec des lettres supplémentaires qui pourraient aider les scientifiques à créer des médicaments, détecter des maladies comme le cancer, ou construire de nouvelles machines biologiques faisant ce que la vie naturelle ne peut pas.

**Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques vont continuer à étudier comment ces lettres d’ADN supplémentaires peuvent être utilisées dans les cellules vivantes et développer de nouvelles technologies basées sur ces codes génétiques élargis. Cela pourrait mener à des avancées en santé, recherche et biologie synthétique.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Des scientifiques ont montré qu’une enzyme vitale peut lire un alphabet ADN à huit lettres, ouvrant la voie à de nouveaux outils et médicaments biologiques.
articles.personality_title_es: Científicos amplían el alfabeto del ADN de 4 a 8 letras, demostrando que una enzima clave puede leer genes sintéticos
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Todos los seres vivos en la Tierra usan ADN hecho de cuatro letras: A, T, C y G. Estas letras forman el código genético que indica a las células cómo funcionar. Los científicos han preguntado durante mucho tiempo si es posible agregar nuevas letras a este código para crear nuevas formas de vida o herramientas.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores de la Universidad de California en San Diego demostraron que una enzima importante llamada ARN polimerasa puede leer ADN con ocho letras en lugar de solo cuatro. Usaron microscopios especiales para observar cómo la enzima lee dos nuevos pares de bases sintéticas que no existen en la naturaleza. La enzima reconoció estas nuevas letras casi igual que las naturales.

**Impacto** – Este descubrimiento significa que las células podrían usar su maquinaria normal para trabajar con nuevos códigos genéticos. Abre la puerta a diseñar ADN con letras extra que podrían ayudar a los científicos a crear medicinas, detectar enfermedades como el cáncer o construir nuevas máquinas biológicas que hagan cosas que la vida natural no puede.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos seguirán explorando cómo estas letras adicionales de ADN pueden usarse en células vivas y desarrollarán nuevas tecnologías basadas en códigos genéticos ampliados. Esto podría llevar a avances en salud, investigación y biología sintética.

**Resumen en una frase** – Científicos demostraron que una enzima vital puede leer un alfabeto de ADN de ocho letras, abriendo el camino para nuevas herramientas y medicinas biológicas.
